note: Generated by sync/build_catalog.py. Catalogue positions are the source of truth: right ascension in hours, declination in degrees, distance in light-years. Cartesian coordinates are derived at load time by CelestialCoordinates.EquatorialToUniverseFromLightYears, in astronomical units, with Earth at the origin. Nothing here is pre-projected or compressed. radiusAstronomicalUnits is the real physical radius of primaryBody; markerAngularSizeDegrees is only a floor on how small the object may look on screen. firstSeen is the day this pipeline first saw the object and never changes afterwards.

objects.fact: Our own star, a yellow dwarf of spectral class G2V.
objects.source: Origin of the map. Every other position is measured from here. Radius is one solar radius.

objects.fact: The closest star system to the Sun, a triple star.
objects.source: ICRS J2000 position; distance from parallax, 1.339 pc. Radius is Alpha Centauri A, 1.223 solar radii.

objects.fact: The brightest star in the night sky, seen from Earth.
objects.source: ICRS J2000 position; distance from parallax, 2.64 pc. Radius is Sirius A, 1.711 solar radii.

objects.fact: So large that, in the Sun's place, it would reach out past the orbit of Mars.
objects.source: ICRS J2000 position. The distance is genuinely uncertain: published values range from roughly 550 to 720 light-years, and 642 is the middle of that spread. Radius ~764 solar radii.

objects.fact: The centre of the Milky Way, with the mass of four million Suns.
objects.source: ICRS J2000 position; distance 8.178 kpc (GRAVITY collaboration). Radius is the Schwarzschild radius for 4.30 million solar masses.

objects.fact: The Milky Way's neighbour, on a collision course in ~4.5 billion years.
objects.source: ICRS J2000 position; distance 778 kpc. Radius is the isophotal disc, about 70 000 light-years, which is what makes it 3.2 degrees wide from Earth.
